title: What Happens to Your Body When You Drink Energy Drinks Every Day
excerpt: From heart rhythm changes to liver damage and a pediatric exposure crisis, here is what medical research says about the health risks of daily energy drink consumption.
body:
• Daily energy drink consumption can cause elevated blood pressure, heart rhythm abnormalities, anxiety, sleep disruption, and potential liver and kidney damage over time, according to research from Harvard, Mayo Clinic, and multiple systematic reviews.
  • Emergency room visits related to caffeine overdose more than doubled for middle school children between 2017 and 2023, with pediatric energy drink exposures rising 24% in a single year.
  • Energy drinks remain unregulated as dietary supplements by the FDA, with some products containing up to 505 mg of caffeine per can — exceeding the 400 mg daily limit recommended for healthy adults.

Energy drinks have become a $60 billion global industry, with brands like Monster, Red Bull, Celsius, and Ghost lining shelves at every gas station and gym. Their popularity has surged across all age groups, but a growing body of medical research is raising alarms about what regular consumption actually does to the human body.

The core concern is straightforward: energy drinks can deliver massive doses of caffeine — along with stimulants like guarana, taurine, and ginseng — far more quickly than coffee or tea. Some products contain over 500 mg of caffeine per can, well above the 400 mg daily limit the FDA considers safe for healthy adults. And unlike coffee, energy drinks are classified as dietary supplements, which means they face no FDA regulation on caffeine content or ingredient disclosure.

What Happens to Your Body

The immediate effects of energy drink consumption are well-documented. Research published in the Journal of the American Heart Association has shown that energy drinks can disrupt normal heart function for hours after consumption. Blood pressure rises, the heart's electrical recharging system is altered, and the risk of potentially life-threatening arrhythmias increases.

According to Mayo Clinic cardiologists, the combination of caffeine, taurine, and guarana affects both the heart's electrical system and its muscular pump. For most people with healthy hearts, an occasional energy drink poses minimal risk. But for the estimated one in 200 people who carry genetic predispositions to sudden cardiac death — conditions like hypertrophic cardiomyopathy or long QT syndrome — the chemicals in energy drinks can be dangerous.

Long-term daily consumption carries additional risks. Mayo Clinic dietitians cite potential damage to the liver and kidneys, chronic hypertension, arterial stiffening, hyperglycemia, weight gain from liquid calories, insulin resistance, and mental health effects from sustained stimulant exposure.

"Caution should be advised for all. While just moderate consumption may be okay, may be safe for some healthy people, it may not be for those with health conditions. The potential risks simply outweigh the benefits."

— Dr. Anna Svatikova, Mayo Clinic

The Youth Crisis

Perhaps the most alarming trend is the rise in energy drink consumption among children and teenagers. According to America's Poison Centers, pediatric exposure to energy drinks among those under 20 rose 24.2% between 2022 and 2023 alone. Most of these cases — 78% — were unintentional, meaning the children didn't realize they were consuming energy drinks or how much caffeine they contained.

Emergency room visits related to caffeine overdose or adverse effects more than doubled for middle school children between 2017 and 2023, according to Harvard Health. There is no established safe level of caffeine consumption for children and adolescents, though the American Academy of Pediatrics recommends teens limit intake to 100 mg per day — less than what many energy drinks contain in a single serving.

A systematic review published in Sports Health analyzing over 92,000 participants found that rates of suicidal ideation were significantly higher among participants who consumed energy drinks more than once daily. Frequent users — defined as five or more energy drinks per week — were also more likely to experience sleep dissatisfaction, persistent depressive mood, and perceived stress.

The Regulatory Gap

Unlike coffee, soft drinks, and medications, energy drinks occupy a regulatory blind spot. By classifying themselves as dietary supplements rather than food or drugs, manufacturers avoid FDA oversight on ingredient amounts, labeling requirements, and safety testing. A Frontiers in Public Health review from researchers at Harvard's T.H. Chan School of Public Health called for restricted sales to children and adolescents and evidence-based caffeine limits.

The challenge is that energy drinks are marketed as lifestyle products — associated with athletic performance, focus, and productivity — making them feel casual and harmless even when their caffeine loads rival or exceed pharmaceutical stimulants.

The Bottom Line

For healthy adults who consume energy drinks occasionally, the risks are likely manageable. But daily consumption, particularly at high volumes, carries documented cardiovascular, metabolic, and mental health risks. For children, teenagers, pregnant women, and anyone with underlying heart conditions, the medical consensus is clear: avoid them entirely. As the industry continues to grow and introduce new formulations, the gap between marketing and medical evidence shows no signs of narrowing.
